result.markdown: --- title: "Continuous-time Markov chains and jump processes" course-unit: ch05-jump-processes status: complete --- ## Where we are | Model | Determinism | Time | State | |---|---|---|---| | ODE (Day 1) | deterministic | continuous | continuous | | Function map (Day 1) | deterministic | discrete | continuous | | Markov chain (Day 1) | stochastic | discrete | discrete | | **Jump process (now)** | **stochastic** | **continuous** | **discrete** | All four are population models: the state is counts, not people. ::: {.notes} Two minutes at the start of the day. These four axes are the map the whole course is drawn on, and today fills in the last population-level corner: stochastic, continuous in time, discrete in state. Point out that the individual-level column is still empty; that is Day 3. ::: ## Why events matter - A CTMC waits for the next infection or recovery. - The state is integer-valued: $X=(S,I,R)$. - Exact event timing exposes fade-out and peak variability. For the baseline population, $$ a_{\mathrm{inf}}=\frac{\beta cSI}{N},\qquad a_{\mathrm{rec}}=\gamma I. $$ ::: {.notes} Contrast this with an ODE: an ODE advances all flows over a numerical interval, while a jump process samples the next event and its type. ::: ## Recap: where the exponential comes from An event with constant hazard $r$ has waiting time $T$ with $$ \Pr(T>t)=e^{-rt},\qquad \Pr(T\le\delta t)=1-e^{-r\delta t}, $$ the same conversion used for the discrete-time chain on Day 1. ::: {.notes} Five minutes, no derivation on the board. Point out that the survival function is where yesterday's rate-to-proportion rule came from: the per-step probability is the chance the waiting time lands inside the step. The full derivation is in the probability prerequisite; nobody needs to have read it to follow this session. ::: ## Recap: memoryless clocks and which one rings first Exponential waiting times are **memoryless**, $$ \Pr(T>s+t\mid T>s)=e^{-rt}=\Pr(T>t), $$ so no per-individual clock has to be carried and the counts $(S,I,R)$ are the whole state. With competing events at rates $a_j$ and $a_0=\sum_j a_j$, $$ \min_j T_j\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(a_0), \qquad \Pr(J=j)=\frac{a_j}{a_0}. $$ ::: {.notes} Memorylessness is a real assumption about the disease: someone infectious for a week is no closer to recovering than someone infected this morning. The two displayed results are the whole Gillespie algorithm: when the next event happens, and which one it is. The next slide is bookkeeping rather than new mathematics. Learners who want the derivations should read the waiting-times section of the probability prerequisite afterwards. ::: ## Gillespie direct algorithm At state $x$, let $a_0=a_{\mathrm{inf}}+a_{\mathrm{rec}}$. 1. Draw $\tau\sim\operatorname{Exponential}(a_0)$. 2. Choose infection with probability $a_{\mathrm{inf}}/a_0$. 3. Apply $(-1,+1,0)$ or $(0,-1,+1)$. This is a stochastic, continuous-time, discrete-state, population-level model. Every event conserves $S+I+R=N$. ::: {.notes} The propensities are rates, not probabilities. The waiting time is continuous even though the state changes by integer increments. ::: ## A visible Julia kernel {.smaller} ::: {#2 .cell execution_count=1} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` gillespie_sir (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} The state update is the stoichiometric change vector in code. The local StableRNG makes the result reproducible without relying on global state. ::: ## One path, and the ODE through it {.center .smaller} ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch04-path .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch04-path .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` One exact CTMC path (steps) against the mean-field ODE (dashed). ::: ::: ::: {.notes} This is the picture the whole morning is about. Every wiggle is a real event, and at a thousand people there are well over a thousand of them, so the steps merge into a rough curve. Zooming in on the first few days is where you would see individual jumps. The dashed curves are yesterday's model, and the gap is not solver error: this particular realization ran a few days late, and a different seed would run early. The title numbers are generated at render time and are realization-specific; conservation is asserted, so a broken kernel would fail the render. Do not let anyone read one path as an expected epidemic; that is the next two slides. ::: ## Recap: two kinds of spread For $M$ independent paths with summary values $z_1,\dots,z_M$, $$ \bar z=\frac1M\sum_k z_k,\qquad s^2=\frac1{M-1}\sum_k (z_k-\bar z)^2,\qquad \operatorname{se}(\bar z)=\frac{s}{\sqrt M}. $$ - The standard deviation $s$ describes **the epidemics**: how much peak size varies. More simulation does not shrink it. - The standard error $\operatorname{se}(\bar z)$ describes **our estimate** of the average, and does shrink, as $1/\sqrt M$: four times the work to halve it. ::: {.notes} Three minutes, and it pays for itself four times today. These two spreads get confused constantly, so keep them apart: one is a property of the disease process, the other a property of how hard we simulated. Say explicitly that this is the vocabulary the rest of the day uses. The relative spread of SDE peaks after the break, the variance-to-mean ratio of case counts this afternoon, and the variance decomposition in the last session all live on this slide. Nobody needs the probability prerequisite for it. ::: ## From model to package API {.smaller} The same reaction structure, in current SciML packages, executed here: ::: {#cell-ch04-catalyst .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#ch04-catalyst .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (3, 201) ``` ::: ::: One rate constant per reaction, so the $\beta cSI/N$ above becomes $\kappa SI$ with $\kappa=\beta c/N$; $R_0=\beta c/\gamma=2$ is unchanged. ::: {.notes} Two reactions in two lines, against the hand-written kernel three slides back. Say that out loud rather than reading the code. The kappa note matters because the book chapter uses kappa from here on: a reaction network carries one rate constant per reaction, and the baseline scenario has not changed. The network also records stoichiometry explicitly, which is what lets the same object become an ODE, an SDE, or a jump model later in the course. ::: ## Twenty paths and the ODE {.center .smaller} ::: {#cell-fig-slide-ch04-ensemble .cell execution_count=1} ::: {#fig-slide-ch04-ensemble .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Twenty CTMC paths of infectious prevalence with the mean-field ODE. ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Five minutes, and let them look before you talk. Two things to point at. First the spread in *timing*: every path has the same shape but peaks somewhere between roughly day 13 and day 25. Second, and this is the one worth labouring: the dashed ODE is not the average of the paths. Its peak is near 158 while the mean of the twenty individual peak heights is around 178, because each path peaks at its own time and averaging asynchronous peaks flattens the curve. So "the ODE peak" and "the average peak of an epidemic" are different quantities. The three numbers in the title are the previous slide made concrete: sd is the epidemics varying, se is how well twenty runs pin the average down. Note that none of these twenty paths fades out. With ten initial infectives and $R_0=2$ that is expected, since fade-out needs all ten introductions to fail. Fade-out is a small-introduction phenomenon, and the worksheet quantifies it. ::: ## Takeaways and links - Propensities determine both waiting times and event probabilities. - Exact jumps preserve integer states and population conservation. - Ensemble summaries are needed for comparison with an ODE.
